tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: kiali_get_logs
tools.description: Get the logs of a Kubernetes Pod (or workload name that will be resolved to a pod) in a namespace. Output is plain text, matching kubernetes-mcp-server pods_log. The line_count field tells you the total number of log lines returned. Analyze ALL of them, but summarize the results unless the user explicitly asks for the raw output. Do not omit any error or warning lines.

container.description: Optional. Name of the Pod container to get the logs from.

format.description: Output formatting for chat. 'codeblock' wraps logs in ~~~ fences (recommended). 'plain' returns raw text like kubernetes-mcp-server pods_log.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the logs from. If it does not exist, it will be treated as a workload name and a running pod will be selected.

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod logs from

previous.description: Optional. Return previous terminated container logs

severity.description: Optional severity filter applied client-side. Accepts 'ERROR', 'WARN' or combinations like 'ERROR,WARN'.

tail.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, defaults to 50). Cannot exceed 200 lines.

workload.description: Optional. Workload name override (used when name lookup fails).

tools.name: kiali_get_mesh_status
tools.description: Retrieves the high-level health, topology, and environment details of the Istio service mesh. Returns multi-cluster control plane status (istiod), data plane namespace health (including ambient mesh status), observability stack health (Prometheus, Grafana...), and component connectivity. Use this tool as the first step to diagnose mesh-wide issues, verify Istio/Kiali versions, or check overall health before drilling into specific workloads.

tools.name: kiali_get_mesh_traffic_graph
tools.description: Returns service-to-service traffic topology, dependencies, and network metrics (throughput, response time, mTLS) for the specified namespaces. Use this to diagnose routing issues, latency, or find upstream/downstream dependencies.

graphType.description: Granularity of the graph. 'app' aggregates by app name, 'versionedApp' separates by versions, 'workload' maps specific pods/deployments. Default: versionedApp.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

namespaces.description: Comma-separated list of namespaces to map

tools.name: kiali_get_metrics
tools.description: Returns a compact JSON summary of Istio metrics (latency quantiles, traffic trends, throughput, payload sizes) for the given resource.

byLabels.description: Comma-separated list of labels to group metrics by (e.g., 'source_workload,destination_service'). Optional

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

quantiles.description: Comma-separated list of quantiles for histogram metrics (e.g., '0.5,0.95,0.99'). Optional

rateInterval.description: Rate interval for metrics (e.g., '1m', '5m'). Optional, defaults to '10m'

reporter.description: Metrics reporter(s). Comma-separated list of: 'source', 'destination', 'waypoint', or the special value 'both' (no reporter filter). Optional, defaults to 'source'. Example: 'source,waypoint'

resourceName.description: Name of the resource to get metrics for

resourceType.description: Type of resource to get metrics

step.description: Step between data points in seconds (e.g., '15'). Optional, defaults to 15 seconds

tools.name: kiali_get_pod_performance
tools.description: Returns a human-readable text summary with current Pod CPU/memory usage (from Prometheus) compared to Kubernetes requests/limits (from the Pod spec). Useful to answer questions like 'Is this workload using too much memory?'

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

podName.description: Kubernetes Pod name. If workloadName is provided, the tool will attempt to resolve a Pod from that workload first.

queryTime.description: Optional end timestamp (RFC3339) for the query. Defaults to now.

timeRange.description: Time window used to compute CPU rate (Prometheus duration like '5m', '10m', '1h', '1d'). Defaults to '10m'.

workloadName.description: Kubernetes Workload name (e.g. Deployment/StatefulSet/etc). Tool will look up the workload and pick one of its Pods. If not found, it will fall back to treating this value as a podName.

tools.name: kiali_get_resource_details
tools.description: Fetches a list of resources OR retrieves detailed data for a specific resource. If 'resourceName' is omitted, it returns a list. If 'resourceName' is provided, it returns details for that specific resource.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

namespaces.description: Comma-separated list of namespaces to query (e.g., 'bookinfo' or 'bookinfo,default'). If not provided, it will query across all accessible namespaces.

resourceName.description: Optional. The specific name of the resource. If left empty, the tool returns a list of all resources of the specified type. If provided, the tool returns deep details for this specific resource.

resourceType.description: The type of resource to query. Use 'app' for Kiali applications (grouped by the Kubernetes 'app' label). Use 'argoapp' for ArgoCD Application CRDs (requires ArgoCD installed and the Kiali service account must have read permissions on applications.argoproj.io).

tools.name: kiali_get_trace_details
tools.description: Fetches a single distributed trace by trace_id and returns its call hierarchy (service tree with duration, status, and nested calls). Use this after list_traces to drill into a specific trace.

traceId.description: Trace ID to fetch and summarize. If provided, namespace/service_name are ignored.

tools.name: kiali_list_mesh_clusters
tools.description: Returns the list of Istio mesh clusters that Kiali can access. Each entry includes its name and whether it is the home cluster (where Kiali is deployed). Call this tool before using meshCluster on other Kiali tools when the target cluster is unknown.

tools.name: kiali_list_traces
tools.description: Lists distributed traces for a service in a namespace. Returns a summary (namespace, service, total_found, avg_duration_ms) and a list of traces with id, duration_ms, spans_count, root_op, slowest_service, has_errors. Use get_trace_details with a trace id to get full hierarchy.

errorOnly.description: If true, only consider traces that contain errors. Default false.

limit.description: Maximum number of traces to return. Default 10.

lookbackSeconds.description: How far back to search. Default 600 (10m).

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

serviceName.description: Service name to search traces for (required). Returns multiple traces up to limit.

tools.name: kiali_manage_istio_config
tools.description: Create, patch, or delete Istio, Gateway API, and Inference API config. Supports Istio resources (networking.istio.io, security.istio.io), Gateway API resources (gateway.networking.k8s.io), and Inference API resources (inference.networking.k8s.io) when installed on the cluster. For list and get (read-only) use manage_istio_config_read.

data.description: JSON or YAML data for the resource. Required for create and patch actions. For create, you can provide partial content (e.g. only spec) and it will be merged onto a valid template with defaults. Arrays (like servers, http, etc.) are REPLACED entirely, so include ALL elements you want.

group.description: API group of the Istio object. Use 'gateway.networking.k8s.io' for Gateway API resources. Use 'inference.networking.k8s.io' for Inference API resources.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

version.description: API version. Use 'v1' for all resource types.

tools.name: kiali_manage_istio_config_read
tools.description: Read Istio, Gateway API, and Inference API config. 'list' groups by namespace→'group/version/kind'→{valid:[...],invalid:[...]} where valid/invalid arrays contain resource names; omit group/kind to retrieve ALL config types in a single call. Supports Istio (networking.istio.io, security.istio.io), Gateway API (gateway.networking.k8s.io), and Inference API (inference.networking.k8s.io) when installed. 'get' returns full YAML. For writes use manage_istio_config.

group.description: API group of the Istio object. Required ONLY for 'get' action. For 'list', OMIT group and kind to retrieve ALL config types in a single call. Use 'gateway.networking.k8s.io' for Gateway API resources. Use 'inference.networking.k8s.io' for Inference API resources.

kind.description: Kind of the Istio object. Required ONLY for 'get' action. For 'list', OMIT to return all kinds at once — do NOT call separately for each kind.

meshCluster.description: Optional Istio mesh cluster name from kiali_list_mesh_clusters (e.g. west). When omitted, Kiali defaults to its home cluster.

namespace.description: Namespace containing the Istio object. For 'list', if not provided, returns objects across all namespaces. For 'get', required.

object.description: Name of the Istio object. Required for 'get' action.

serviceName.description: Filter Istio configurations (VirtualServices, DestinationRules, and their referenced Gateways) that affect a specific service. Only applicable for 'list' action

version.description: API version. Use 'v1' for all resource types. Required for 'get' action.

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

Done. Here’s what I set up and changed:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in canary-deployment-ns
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80, security config matches stable (no extra securityContext)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine to target both stable and canary
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
  - Port remains 80 -> targetPort 8080 (matches existing service behavior)

Traffic split
- With 2 replicas for engine-v2-0 and 2 for engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across endpoints.
- Note: If either deployment scales unevenly, the share will shift. For precise weighting, use a traffic manager (e.g., Istio) with weights.

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine (should list pods from both versions)
- Send a few requests and check which pod answers:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns logs deploy/engine-v2-0 --tail=20
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns logs deploy/engine-v2-1 --tail=20

Rollback/adjustments
- To revert to stable only: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or scale the canary to 0.
- To bias traffic: adjust replica counts (e.g., stable 3, canary 1 ≈ 75/25).

- With 2 replicas for engine-v2-0 and 2 for engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across endpoints.
- Note: If either deployment scales unevenly, the share will shift. For precise weighting, use a traffic manager (e.g., Istio) with weights.

- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine (should list pods from both versions)

  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns logs deploy/engine-v2-0 --tail=20
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns logs deploy/engine-v2-1 --tail=20

Rollback/adjustments
- To revert to stable only: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or scale the canary to 0.

Traffic split
- With 2 replicas for engine-v2-0 and 2 for engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across endpoints.
- Note: If either deployment scales unevenly, the share will shift. For precise weighting, use a traffic manager (e.g., Istio) with weights.

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine (should list pods from both versions)
- Send a few requests and check which pod answers:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns logs deploy/engine-v2-0 --tail=20
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns logs deploy/engine-v2-1 --tail=20

Rollback/adjustments
- To revert to stable only: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0, or scale the canary to 0.
- To bias traffic: adjust replica counts (e.g., stable 3, canary 1 ≈ 75/25).

results.taskOutput:
I found the root cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container command to run: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command
- That command doesn’t exist, so the container exited immediately and the pod went into BackOff.

What I changed
- Replaced the faulty Deployment with a clean spec that uses the image’s default command (no command/args override).
- Set containerPort to 8080 (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: app-5c7bd5bd8f-cqn2b 1/1 Running, 0 restarts
- Deployment app in crashloop-test has 1 available replica and no BackOff events.

Want me to also expose it via a Service (ClusterIP/LoadBalancer) or add readiness/liveness probes?

outputSteps.content:
I found the root cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container command to run: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command
- That command doesn’t exist, so the container exited immediately and the pod went into BackOff.

What I changed
- Replaced the faulty Deployment with a clean spec that uses the image’s default command (no command/args override).
- Set containerPort to 8080 (nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: app-5c7bd5bd8f-cqn2b 1/1 Running, 0 restarts
- Deployment app in crashloop-test has 1 available replica and no BackOff events.

Want me to also expose it via a Service (ClusterIP/LoadBalancer) or add readiness/liveness probes?

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

- Root cause: The Deployment debug/app was using an invalid image tag: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag, causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.
- Action taken: Updated the Deployment to use a valid image: docker.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable-alpine (server-side apply).
- Current state:
  - Pod app-96469c9-wckb6 is Running (1/1).
  - Deployment app is Available with 1/1 ready replica.
  - Events confirm the new image pulled successfully and the old ReplicaSet was scaled down.

If you prefer a different image source or need it pinned by digest, say the word and I’ll update it (e.g., quay.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable-alpine or nginx:stable). Would you like me to keep using Docker Hub or switch back to a Quay.io image?

results.taskOutput:
I found the cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". The scheduler reported “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

What I changed
- Deleted the Pending PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it was never bound).
- Recreated the PVC using the existing default StorageClass "standard".

Result
- A volume was dynamically provisioned and bound to homepage-pvc.
- The pod homepage-pod is now Running:
  - Phase: Running
  - Node: mcp-eval-cluster
  - Container: nginx started and Ready

Notes
- This created a brand-new empty volume at /usr/share/nginx/html. If you expected existing site content, we can populate the PVC or switch to the desired StorageClass if you want a different backend.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I found the cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". The scheduler reported “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

What I changed
- Deleted the Pending PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it was never bound).
- Recreated the PVC using the existing default StorageClass "standard".

Result
- A volume was dynamically provisioned and bound to homepage-pvc.
- The pod homepage-pod is now Running:
  - Phase: Running
  - Node: mcp-eval-cluster
  - Container: nginx started and Ready

Notes
- This created a brand-new empty volume at /usr/share/nginx/html. If you expected existing site content, we can populate the PVC or switch to the desired StorageClass if you want a different backend.

outputSteps.content:
I found the cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". The scheduler reported “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

What I changed
- Deleted the Pending PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it was never bound).
- Recreated the PVC using the existing default StorageClass "standard".

Result
- A volume was dynamically provisioned and bound to homepage-pvc.
- The pod homepage-pod is now Running:
  - Phase: Running
  - Node: mcp-eval-cluster
  - Container: nginx started and Ready

Notes
- This created a brand-new empty volume at /usr/share/nginx/html. If you expected existing site content, we can populate the PVC or switch to the desired StorageClass if you want a different backend.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed your webapp in the orders namespace.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080 by default, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing connection refused.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app even when it was up.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080 (readiness and liveness).
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 internally).

Current status (verified)
- Pod: webapp-9747b66b4-85s5q is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service: orders/webapp now targets port 8080 and has a healthy endpoint:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.38:8080 (pod webapp-9747b66b4-85s5q)
- Events show no new probe failures for the new pod.

How to test (in-cluster)
- From another pod: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local:80

Would you like me to:
- Expose it externally (Ingress/Route/LoadBalancer)?
- Clean up the container’s unused port 80 entry to avoid confusion?

Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I investigated and fixed your webapp in the orders namespace.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080 by default, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing connection refused.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app even when it was up.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080 (readiness and liveness).
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 internally).

Current status (verified)
- Pod: webapp-9747b66b4-85s5q is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service: orders/webapp now targets port 8080 and has a healthy endpoint:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.38:8080 (pod webapp-9747b66b4-85s5q)
- Events show no new probe failures for the new pod.

How to test (in-cluster)
- From another pod: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local:80

Would you like me to:
- Expose it externally (Ingress/Route/LoadBalancer)?
- Clean up the container’s unused port 80 entry to avoid confusion?

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed your webapp in the orders namespace.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080 by default, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting port 80 on non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing connection refused.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app even when it was up.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080 (readiness and liveness).
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 internally).

Current status (verified)
- Pod: webapp-9747b66b4-85s5q is 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service: orders/webapp now targets port 8080 and has a healthy endpoint:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.38:8080 (pod webapp-9747b66b4-85s5q)
- Events show no new probe failures for the new pod.

How to test (in-cluster)
- From another pod: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local:80

Would you like me to:
- Expose it externally (Ingress/Route/LoadBalancer)?
- Clean up the container’s unused port 80 entry to avoid confusion?

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to pod-reader (pod-reader-role) did not grant permissions on core/v1 pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments, so the service account could not list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: '' (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing permission to list deployments.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
  - Expected: yes
- Try listing pods in the namespace:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you tried --all-namespaces before, that will still be forbidden. If you need cluster-wide read of pods, I can create a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding for you.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to pod-reader (pod-reader-role) did not grant permissions on core/v1 pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments, so the service account could not list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: '' (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing permission to list deployments.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
  - Expected: yes
- Try listing pods in the namespace:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you tried --all-namespaces before, that will still be forbidden. If you need cluster-wide read of pods, I can create a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding for you.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to pod-reader (pod-reader-role) did not grant permissions on core/v1 pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments, so the service account could not list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: '' (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing permission to list deployments.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
  - Expected: yes
- Try listing pods in the namespace:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you tried --all-namespaces before, that will still be forbidden. If you need cluster-wide read of pods, I can create a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding for you.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Service had a selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web but the nginx pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: the Service had no endpoints and wasn’t routing traffic.
- Target port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root), but the Service was targeting port 80. Even with endpoints, that would fail.

What I changed
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080
- Verified endpoints now exist: 10.244.0.40:8080
- Launched a short-lived test pod and confirmed:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ → returns nginx default HTML
  - curl http://10.101.133.141/ → returns nginx default HTML

Current status
- The nginx Service is healthy and accessible inside the cluster at:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local (port 80)
  - http://10.101.133.141 (port 80)

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP and there is no Ingress configured in namespace web. If you need access from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - LoadBalancer Service (cloud environments)
  - Ingress (requires an Ingress Controller; provide a hostname)
  - NodePort (simple, but exposes a high port on each node)

Tell me which option you prefer (and hostname if using Ingress), and I’ll set it up. Also, I can remove the temporary nettool-test pod if you’d like.

namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Service had a selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web but the nginx pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: the Service had no endpoints and wasn’t routing traffic.
- Target port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root), but the Service was targeting port 80. Even with endpoints, that would fail.

What I changed
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080
- Verified endpoints now exist: 10.244.0.40:8080
- Launched a short-lived test pod and confirmed:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ → returns nginx default HTML
  - curl http://10.101.133.141/ → returns nginx default HTML

- The nginx Service is healthy and accessible inside the cluster at:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local (port 80)
  - http://10.101.133.141 (port 80)

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP and there is no Ingress configured in namespace web. If you need access from outside the cluster, choose one:

  - NodePort (simple, but exposes a high port on each node)

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Service had a selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web but the nginx pods are labeled app=nginx. Result: the Service had no endpoints and wasn’t routing traffic.
- Target port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (non-root), but the Service was targeting port 80. Even with endpoints, that would fail.

What I changed
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080
- Verified endpoints now exist: 10.244.0.40:8080
- Launched a short-lived test pod and confirmed:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ → returns nginx default HTML
  - curl http://10.101.133.141/ → returns nginx default HTML

Current status
- The nginx Service is healthy and accessible inside the cluster at:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local (port 80)
  - http://10.101.133.141 (port 80)

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP and there is no Ingress configured in namespace web. If you need access from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - LoadBalancer Service (cloud environments)
  - Ingress (requires an Ingress Controller; provide a hostname)
  - NodePort (simple, but exposes a high port on each node)

Tell me which option you prefer (and hostname if using Ingress), and I’ll set it up. Also, I can remove the temporary nettool-test pod if you’d like.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of what was wrong
- Your web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any node: environment=production-gpu. With no pods running, the Service had no endpoints, so requests to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local failed with connection refused.
- Additionally, the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged typically listens on port 8080. The Service originally targeted port 80, which would also have caused connection refused even if pods were running.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the mismatched nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (so pods can schedule on the available node).
- Exposed the container on port 8080 and updated the Service to keep port 80 for clients but targetPort 8080 on the pods.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-54fb75bcb8-2f62j (10.244.0.44)
  - web-app-deployment-54fb75bcb8-zzl2j (10.244.0.43)
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.43:8080, 10.244.0.44:8080
- Pod logs show nginx starting normally; no errors.

Validation you can run
- From any pod in the cluster: curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or: kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward svc/web-app-service 8080:80 and curl http://localhost:8080

Notes and next steps
- If you intended to pin these pods to specific nodes, either:
  - Label the target node and reintroduce nodeSelector (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Use a different, correct label/toleration that matches your cluster.
- Consider adding readiness/liveness probes, resource requests/limits, and pinning the image tag instead of latest to improve reliability.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of what was wrong
- Your web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any node: environment=production-gpu. With no pods running, the Service had no endpoints, so requests to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local failed with connection refused.
- Additionally, the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged typically listens on port 8080. The Service originally targeted port 80, which would also have caused connection refused even if pods were running.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the mismatched nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (so pods can schedule on the available node).
- Exposed the container on port 8080 and updated the Service to keep port 80 for clients but targetPort 8080 on the pods.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-54fb75bcb8-2f62j (10.244.0.44)
  - web-app-deployment-54fb75bcb8-zzl2j (10.244.0.43)
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.43:8080, 10.244.0.44:8080
- Pod logs show nginx starting normally; no errors.

Validation you can run
- From any pod in the cluster: curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or: kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward svc/web-app-service 8080:80 and curl http://localhost:8080

Notes and next steps
- If you intended to pin these pods to specific nodes, either:
  - Label the target node and reintroduce nodeSelector (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Use a different, correct label/toleration that matches your cluster.
- Consider adding readiness/liveness probes, resource requests/limits, and pinning the image tag instead of latest to improve reliability.

Let me know if you want me to reapply a nodeSelector with a label that actually exists on your nodes, or add health probes.

Done.

- Namespace: multi-container-logging (exists)
- Pod: communication-pod

  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged (port 8080), readinessProbe http GET / on port http

Done.

What I created
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) for stable networking
- StatefulSet: db with 3 replicas
  - Container: busybox:1.36 (sleep infinity)
  - initContainer writes /data/test with contents: initial_data (only if not already present)
  - volumeClaimTemplates: 1Gi RWO PVC per pod, mounted at /data
- Scaled StatefulSet db back down to 1 replica

Notes
- The StatefulSet now targets 1 replica; it will converge as the controller completes scale-down. PVCs for db-1 and db-2 are retained (persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy=Retain), so if you scale back up later their data will still be there.

How to verify
- Check scaling state:
  - kubectl get sts db -n statefulset-test
- List pods:
  - kubectl get pods -n statefulset-test -l app=db
- Confirm data in a remaining pod (e.g., db-0):
  - kubectl exec -n statefulset-test db-0 -- cat /data/test
  - Expected output: initial_data
- See the retained PVCs:
  - kubectl get pvc -n statefulset-test -l app=db

Here’s what the data shows.

Where time is spent (distributed traces):
- Traces found: 10; avg duration ~2.57s. Two slow classes observed: ~2.5–3.0s and one at ~10s.
- Representative 10.0s trace (id 84695d…):
  - Path: istio-ingressgateway -> productpage -> details (≈1–2ms, 200) -> reviews (≈3.0s, then nested call) -> ratings (≈10.0s, http.status_code=0).
  - Most of the time is in reviews -> ratings.
- Representative 2.53s trace (id 8554ec…):
  - Path: productpage -> details (≈1–2ms, 200) -> reviews (≈2.52s) -> ratings (≈2.50s, http.status_code=0).
  - Again, time is in reviews -> ratings.
- Notes:
  - details is consistently fast.
  - The http.status_code=0 on the ratings span indicates the upstream request did not complete (likely client-side timeout/cancel), which explains why productpage still returns 200 while incurring delay.

Istio config affecting this path (bookinfo namespace):
- VirtualService bookinfo
  - Hosts: “*”; Gateways: bookinfo-gateway
  - Routes “/productpage” to productpage:9080
  - No delays/faults/timeouts here.
- VirtualService ratings
  - Hosts: ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local
  - http:
    - route to destination host ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local subset v1
    - fault:
      - delay: fixedDelay: 25s
      - percentage: 100%
- DestinationRule ratings
  - Host: ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local
  - subsets:
    - v1: labels version=v1
  - No trafficPolicy (no LB/outlier/connection pool overrides).
- No VirtualService/DestinationRule for reviews were found.

Correlation of mesh config to the observed delay:
- Every request to ratings v1 is configured to incur a 25s artificial delay (VirtualService ratings fault delay 25s at 100%).
- Traces show reviews -> ratings calls hanging for 2.5s or ~10s and then returning with http.status_code=0 (no response), which is consistent with application/Envoy timeouts aborting before the full 25s delay completes.
  - This produces end-to-end productpage latency spikes matching the waiting period on the ratings call (roughly 2.5s or 10s in the samples).

Most likely root cause:
- An intentional Istio fault injection on the ratings VirtualService (25s fixed delay at 100%) is causing the reviews -> ratings call to stall until client-side timeouts trigger, leading to productpage latency spikes.

Recommendation:
- Remove or reduce the VirtualService ratings fault delay (or set percentage to 0) if this is not desired testing behavior.
- Optionally align client timeouts/retries/fallbacks in reviews if retaining any delay for testing.

Steps.message:
Here’s what the data shows.

Where time is spent (distributed traces):
- Traces found: 10; avg duration ~2.57s. Two slow classes observed: ~2.5–3.0s and one at ~10s.
- Representative 10.0s trace (id 84695d…):
  - Path: istio-ingressgateway -> productpage -> details (≈1–2ms, 200) -> reviews (≈3.0s, then nested call) -> ratings (≈10.0s, http.status_code=0).
  - Most of the time is in reviews -> ratings.
- Representative 2.53s trace (id 8554ec…):
  - Path: productpage -> details (≈1–2ms, 200) -> reviews (≈2.52s) -> ratings (≈2.50s, http.status_code=0).
  - Again, time is in reviews -> ratings.
- Notes:
  - details is consistently fast.
  - The http.status_code=0 on the ratings span indicates the upstream request did not complete (likely client-side timeout/cancel), which explains why productpage still returns 200 while incurring delay.

Istio config affecting this path (bookinfo namespace):
- VirtualService bookinfo
  - Hosts: “*”; Gateways: bookinfo-gateway
  - Routes “/productpage” to productpage:9080
  - No delays/faults/timeouts here.
- VirtualService ratings
  - Hosts: ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local
  - http:
    - route to destination host ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local subset v1
    - fault:
      - delay: fixedDelay: 25s
      - percentage: 100%
- DestinationRule ratings
  - Host: ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local
  - subsets:
    - v1: labels version=v1
  - No trafficPolicy (no LB/outlier/connection pool overrides).
- No VirtualService/DestinationRule for reviews were found.

Correlation of mesh config to the observed delay:
- Every request to ratings v1 is configured to incur a 25s artificial delay (VirtualService ratings fault delay 25s at 100%).
- Traces show reviews -> ratings calls hanging for 2.5s or ~10s and then returning with http.status_code=0 (no response), which is consistent with application/Envoy timeouts aborting before the full 25s delay completes.
  - This produces end-to-end productpage latency spikes matching the waiting period on the ratings call (roughly 2.5s or 10s in the samples).

Most likely root cause:
- An intentional Istio fault injection on the ratings VirtualService (25s fixed delay at 100%) is causing the reviews -> ratings call to stall until client-side timeouts trigger, leading to productpage latency spikes.

Recommendation:
- Remove or reduce the VirtualService ratings fault delay (or set percentage to 0) if this is not desired testing behavior.
- Optionally align client timeouts/retries/fallbacks in reviews if retaining any delay for testing.

Here’s what the data shows.

Where time is spent (distributed traces):
- Traces found: 10; avg duration ~2.57s. Two slow classes observed: ~2.5–3.0s and one at ~10s.
- Representative 10.0s trace (id 84695d…):
  - Path: istio-ingressgateway -> productpage -> details (≈1–2ms, 200) -> reviews (≈3.0s, then nested call) -> ratings (≈10.0s, http.status_code=0).
  - Most of the time is in reviews -> ratings.
- Representative 2.53s trace (id 8554ec…):
  - Path: productpage -> details (≈1–2ms, 200) -> reviews (≈2.52s) -> ratings (≈2.50s, http.status_code=0).
  - Again, time is in reviews -> ratings.
- Notes:
  - details is consistently fast.
  - The http.status_code=0 on the ratings span indicates the upstream request did not complete (likely client-side timeout/cancel), which explains why productpage still returns 200 while incurring delay.

Istio config affecting this path (bookinfo namespace):
- VirtualService bookinfo
  - Hosts: “*”; Gateways: bookinfo-gateway
  - Routes “/productpage” to productpage:9080
  - No delays/faults/timeouts here.
- VirtualService ratings
  - Hosts: ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local
  - http:
    - route to destination host ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local subset v1
    - fault:
      - delay: fixedDelay: 25s
      - percentage: 100%
- DestinationRule ratings
  - Host: ratings.bookinfo.svc.cluster.local
  - subsets:
    - v1: labels version=v1
  - No trafficPolicy (no LB/outlier/connection pool overrides).
- No VirtualService/DestinationRule for reviews were found.

Correlation of mesh config to the observed delay:
- Every request to ratings v1 is configured to incur a 25s artificial delay (VirtualService ratings fault delay 25s at 100%).
- Traces show reviews -> ratings calls hanging for 2.5s or ~10s and then returning with http.status_code=0 (no response), which is consistent with application/Envoy timeouts aborting before the full 25s delay completes.
  - This produces end-to-end productpage latency spikes matching the waiting period on the ratings call (roughly 2.5s or 10s in the samples).

Most likely root cause:
- An intentional Istio fault injection on the ratings VirtualService (25s fixed delay at 100%) is causing the reviews -> ratings call to stall until client-side timeouts trigger, leading to productpage latency spikes.

Recommendation:
- Remove or reduce the VirtualService ratings fault delay (or set percentage to 0) if this is not desired testing behavior.
- Optionally align client timeouts/retries/fallbacks in reviews if retaining any delay for testing.
